prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators, and for the first experimental observation of helical edge transport in HgTe quantum wells.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B016 as my preferred single-part prize. The reasons are unchanged but sharper. Kane and Mele made a sharp, falsifiable prediction: a time-reversal-invariant insulator can carry a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states. Molenkamp's group tested it in HgTe wells in 2007, and the effect has since been reproduced in other material platforms for almost two decades. The achievement changed how we classify band structure, and it feeds directly into topological superconductivity and Majorana-based device ideas, which matters to me as someone working on superconducting circuits. The round-1 files show that B014 and B016 are both mature and independently reproduced, so maturity does not separate them. What separates them is the kind of result being honoured. I weigh a new classification of electronic matter, with a closed prediction-and-observation loop, above a precision-measurement invention whose main outcome is smaller uncertainty on a known quantity. The chair asked what would move me to B014: a finding that the HgTe attribution cannot be defended in a three-name citation, or a committee judgement that 2016 already covers this ground. I do not currently hold either view, but I would move without difficulty, since B014 is my honest second choice and has the cleaner credit.
statement.case_against: The credit remains the weak point. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe platform that Molenkamp actually tested, Zhang is deceased, and the three-name ceiling leaves Bernevig and Hughes unrecognised. The citation is worded around Molenkamp's observation rather than the proposal, which helps, but the omission is not costless. The 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane and Mele; Moore and Balents; Hasan) lies outside this candidate and a reader may find the story incomplete. HgTe edge conductance is imperfectly quantised in longer channels, so the experiment confirms the helical edge picture less cleanly than the early reports suggested, although later work in other materials supports the physics. B014, by contrast, offers a two-person credit with no credited person obviously missing from the core, and has the broader opening support. These are real costs and I do not wish to dismiss them.

responses.point: Kroll holds B014 first on the grounds that the magic-wavelength idea is an independent invention, that 1e-18 performance is reproduced across laboratories, and that overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a fair challenge but not decisive.
responses.response: I accept that the magic-wavelength idea is original and that the Katori and Ye split is clean, and I do not think B014 is a prize that would embarrass the committee. Where I still differ is on what is new in nature. The lattice clock combines the comb, narrow-line laser cooling and a clever cancellation of a differential light shift, and its value lies in measurement performance. The chair asked what criterion should decide between B014 and B016. Mine is conceptual reach together with a closed prediction-and-confirmation loop, and on that criterion B016 is ahead. I also note that the SI redefinition is a timing argument, and I would not use it against B014 or in favour of B016. If the committee prefers instrumental invention with clean credit over conceptual reclassification, I would not oppose B014 and would vote it second.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a specific invention with its own physics (control of differential light shifts, narrow transitions, many-body effects), that its credit is as clean as the shortlist offers, and that the concept-versus-performance split is the normal pattern for an instrument prize.
responses.response: I find the atomic-physics argument convincing as a description of B014, and I agree that a concept-plus-performance split is how instrument prizes usually work. My remaining hesitation is the ion-clock and Yb lattice groups she herself mentions, since the accuracy race involved many teams and the two-name credit will exclude some of them. I do not see that as disqualifying. It is a similar problem to the missing HgTe proposers in B016, so I will not claim that B016's attribution is better, only that its scientific consequence is a classification of phases of matter rather than a better number. I also accept her point that fundamental physics includes what we can measure and how well, so this is a real choice between two good prizes and not a matter of one being weak.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B016 after reading the ballots, citing the full prediction-to-observation chain, the stability of results across materials, and the view that Z2 insulators are distinct from the 2016 topological phase transition prize, while admitting the imperfect HgTe quantisation and incomplete credit.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the chain and of 2016: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz honoured topological defects, quantised Hall conductance and the Chern insulator, while Z2 insulators with time-reversal symmetry and protected helical edges are a separate step. We both name the weak quantisation in HgTe. I would add a caution about how much weight to put on it. The experiment saw edge-dominated conduction and nonlocal transport in the expected regime, and the physics has been confirmed elsewhere, so the imperfect plateau is a limit on the HgTe device, not on the effect. Where I am more cautious than he is is on whether B016's lead in opening support is robust. Seven rankings are broad but B014's all-eight ranking is broader, and we should not read either count as a scientific argument.

responses.point: Danielsson puts B016 first as an unusually complete theory-to-experiment chain, flags the omitted HgTe proposers and the 2016 overlap, and leaves open that the overlap could move him to B014.
responses.response: I share his view of the chain and his worry about 2016, and I think his own hesitation is the right test. My answer on the overlap is that 2016 rewarded topological phase transitions and quantised transport in Haldane-type systems, and the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators is a distinct subject, so I would not move to B014 on that ground alone. Where we should be honest with each other is that if a majority of the committee believes the overlap is serious, the credit gap and the overlap together would make B014 the more defensible public position. I would then have to weigh that outcome, and I would want the citation to state the Z2 classification and helical edge transport explicitly so the distinction from 2016 is visible.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B016 low because the credit set leaves out significant parts of the field and the 2016 prize makes the timing less compelling, and she moved from B042 to B014 after reading the other ballots.
responses.response: I take the credit concern seriously and have no complete answer to it, since three names cannot cover Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Bernevig, Hughes and the 3D work. I think the argument for B016 is that it honours a single closed chain, not a whole field, and that the omissions are a feature of the three-name rule that applies to every shortlisted candidate (B014 has its own, with Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and others). On 2016 I disagree on the weight: a prize is defined by the discovery honoured, not by the word topological. I note her possible Japanese institutional link to Katori that she has to check; for me that is a disclosure matter that the committee can settle without affecting the scientific comparison.

responses.point: As chair, Pearce moved from B021 to B014 after reading the ballots and asks which criterion should decide between B014 and B016 and what would move members from one to the other.
responses.response: I will answer his question directly. I would decide by conceptual reach and a closed prediction-and-confirmation loop, then check attribution, and use opening support only as a tie-breaker. On the first two B016 comes out ahead for me, on the third B014 does. What would move me to B014 is a committee finding that the HgTe attribution cannot be defended or that 2016 makes B016 redundant; I would then support B014 without reluctance. I also take his earlier view that B017 is early seriously, and I agree it should stay an alternative, since the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is unsettled.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-name credit that omits Bernevig and Hughes, given that the HgTe proposal preceded Molenkamp's observation and that Zhang is deceased.
Whether the 2016 topological prize is read as covering Z2 insulators, which would make B016 redundant in the committee's eyes.

How to weigh B014's wider opening support and clean two-person credit against B016's conceptual reach, and whether a precision-measurement invention or a new classification of matter better fits the Prize's tradition.
I rely on general knowledge of priority history in HgTe, 3D topological insulators and lattice-clock competition, and have not verified chronology details against the nomination files.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B016 or B014 from my profile; I work in superconducting circuits, not atomic clocks or HgTe transport. A conflict does arise for B009 (circuit QED): I work in superconducting circuits and waveguide QED at Chalmers, direct WACQT, and have documented ties to Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, so I would recuse myself or at least decline to advocate there. The 2025 laureates also visited Chalmers, which is a proximity concern for any superconducting-circuit candidate. My disclosure is unchanged since round 1.
